2bab2f3b28:
The second capstone moves from the API and Agent SDK to Claude Code itself. Three of the official scenarios live here: Code Generation with Claude Code, Developer Productivity, and Claude Code for Continuous Integration.

These scenarios rarely ask "what does flag X do". They describe a team symptom and ask which configuration change fixes it. A new hire's Claude ignores the test conventions. A CI review posts the same comment on every push. A reviewer is thorough on two files and superficial on eight.

To answer reliably, you need to know where each kind of instruction lives, when it's loaded, who shares it, and which mechanisms are deterministic.
0437954049:
The project is a small Java 21 / Spring Boot 3 order-service with a React + TypeScript order console. It's the kind of repository a platform team at a retailer or telecom would own.

We configure it for a team of developers using Claude Code, then add a headless, multi-pass review job in GitHub Actions. An offline pytest suite checks everything, so you can prove the configuration works before spending a token.
c4e74bb226:
As in Capstone A, start by sorting requirements by kind. The exam keeps asking you to choose between a prompt-level mechanism (CLAUDE.md, a rule, a command) and a deterministic one (a permission rule, a hook, a schema).

The question to ask is the one you'd ask about any distributed system: must this always hold, or should it usually hold?
53ab6afd1a:
The split mirrors what a Spring team already does. Coding conventions live in a wiki and in code review: guidance, usually followed. Things that must never happen live in the CI pipeline, branch protection and IAM: enforcement, always.

CLAUDE.md and rules are the wiki. Permissions and hooks are the branch protection. A schema on the CI output is the API contract.
75a4579362:
Read the figure by row.

The top row is scope: who sees a setting. User scope (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ~/.claude/settings.json) follows one developer across all repositories. Project scope is committed and shared. Local scope (CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/settings.local.json) is the developer's private override for this repository.

The classic exam symptom is "the new team member's Claude does not follow our conventions". It almost always means the conventions were written in someone's user or local file instead of the project file.
6e04e7ef10:
The second row is guidance. CLAUDE.md is loaded at session start. Imports pull other files in as if pasted. Rules under .claude/rules/ without a paths field load like CLAUDE.md. With paths, they load only when Claude works with a matching file.

The third row is workflows, which only enter context when someone invokes them.

The fourth row is enforcement. Permission rules, hooks and MCP configuration are read by the Claude Code harness, not by the model. So they hold whatever the model decides.
3643dc8be8:
The Java and TypeScript code is deliberately ordinary: a controller, a service with an OrderStatus.canTransitionTo state machine, an in-memory repository, two Flyway migrations, and two React components, each with a sibling test.

The point of the capstone is the Claude Code layer around it. Ordinary code makes the review criteria concrete. The canned findings in the test fixtures refer to real lines in OrderController.java and OrderService.java.
e9c0868284:
CLAUDE.md is the team's standing briefing. It's loaded into the context at the start of every session, and that has two consequences.

First, everything in it costs tokens in every conversation. So it should hold what's relevant to most tasks: commands, hard rules, pointers.

Second, it's guidance. The model reads it and usually follows it, but nothing outside the model checks compliance.
f054baf8f3:
The @docs/standards/architecture.md lines are imports. Claude Code expands them when it loads the file. So the standards live once, in the docs folder where humans also read them, and the CLAUDE.md stays short.

This is the "modular organisation" half of task 3.1: one topic per file, imported where needed. Compare that with a 600-line CLAUDE.md that nobody maintains. Imports are relative to the file containing them, and can nest a few levels deep.
3daa8f0d26:
The other half of 3.1 is the hierarchy. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md files from the user directory, from the project root, and from parent and child directories of where you work.

In a monorepo you can put frontend specifics in a web/CLAUDE.md. It's picked up when Claude reads files under web/. More specific files add to the general ones rather than replacing them.

When instructions conflict, the model is told to prefer the more specific location. The cleaner answer, though, is to avoid conflicts by keeping each fact in exactly one place.
1afc500ac8: Use /memory inside a session to see which memory files are loaded. It's the first diagnostic step when someone says Claude "ignores" a convention. Check whether the file is loaded at all before you reword it.
6da34033a8:
Some conventions apply only to some files. Test conventions matter when editing tests. Migration rules matter when touching db/migration. Putting them all in CLAUDE.md wastes context on every unrelated task, and dilutes attention.

A rule file with a paths frontmatter field fixes this. It loads only when Claude works with a file that matches one of its globs.
78b7fef439:
The exam's favourite comparison is a path rule versus a directory CLAUDE.md.

Tests in this repository are colocated. OrderTable.test.tsx sits next to OrderTable.tsx, in a different folder for every component. A web/src/components/CLAUDE.md would load for production components too. A tests/CLAUDE.md would never load, because there's no tests folder.

Only a glob over the file name, **/*.test.tsx, says "every test file, wherever it lives".
a32929bc34:
Globs are where silent mistakes happen. *.test.tsx without **/ may match only at the root. src/**/api matches the directory but not the files inside it.

So the test suite parses every rule's frontmatter and checks each glob against files it must and must not match. It uses gitignore-style semantics: **/ is zero or more directories, and * stays inside one segment.
99c7dbb5ca:
Two tests carry most of the value.

test_every_rule_matches_at_least_one_real_file catches a rule whose glob was mistyped so it never loads. Without the test, that failure is invisible.

test_every_component_has_colocated_test enforces the "every component ships with a sibling test" rule mechanically. The rule file becomes guidance for Claude, and the test becomes the guarantee.
0f666fc2b0:
Everything so far is text in the context window. The model weighs it against everything else and usually complies. For the requirements labelled "invariant", that's not enough.

Claude Code has two mechanisms the model can't talk its way past: permission rules and hooks.
03f9617e6e:
The harness evaluates permission rules before a tool runs. deny wins over ask, which wins over allow.

  • The allow list removes friction for safe, frequent actions: running tests, reading code.
  • The ask list keeps a human in the loop for actions with side effects outside the working tree (git push, editing migrations).
  • The deny list makes secrets unreadable.

This file is committed, so every developer gets the same guard rails. A developer can loosen them only in their own settings.local.json. An organisation can pin them with managed settings that individuals can't override.
1ad2dd5536: Permission patterns match the shape of a call, not its meaning. Bash(rm -rf:*) doesn't catch rm -fr, rm -r -f, or find . -delete. That's why the destructive-command rules also live in a hook, where you can write real logic.
8e417f8913:
The hook uses both blocking styles on purpose, so you can see the difference.

Exit code 2 is the blunt instrument. The call is blocked, and whatever was on stderr goes back to Claude as the reason.

Exit 0 with a permissionDecision: "deny" JSON object is the structured form. It carries a reason the model can act on ("use expand/contract across releases"). The same JSON channel can also return allow or ask.

Any other non-zero exit is a non-blocking error: the user sees it, and the call proceeds. That's why invalid input exits 1 rather than 2. A broken hook should be noticed, not silently freeze every tool call.
442bbef503: The Spring analogy is a servlet filter in front of every controller. The controller (the model) can be as well written as you like. The filter is where you put the check that must run on every request. And like a filter, the hook is ordinary code you can unit test without starting the application.
0e6fcf968a:
The PostToolUse hook is the other half. format.sh runs google-java-format or prettier on the file just edited.

That turns "please format code like this" from a CLAUDE.md line, which costs tokens and is sometimes ignored, into a step that always happens. It also lets the review criteria say "do not report formatting" with confidence.
15f3e8def8:
A project-scoped .mcp.json is committed, so every developer gets the same servers.

Secrets never go into it. ${GITHUB_TOKEN} is expanded from each developer's environment (and from the CI secret store) when the server starts.

Claude Code asks each user to approve project-scoped servers the first time. Otherwise a committed file could start arbitrary processes on a developer's machine. Personal servers go in user scope with claude mcp add --scope user, and they aren't committed.
b60397aa8f:
Task 2.5 is about choosing and restricting tools.

For exploration, the built-in Grep (content search), Glob (find files by pattern) and Read are cheaper and safer than shelling out to grep or find. They can't modify anything, and their output is shaped for the model.

Edit makes targeted string replacements. Prefer it over Write for existing files, because a rewritten file can silently drop content.

Every workflow in this repository states the smallest tool set it needs:
d927a423f7:
A slash command is a saved prompt with metadata. Files in .claude/commands/ are shared through git. Files in ~/.claude/commands/ are personal.

$ARGUMENTS is replaced with what the user typed after the command. argument-hint shows in autocomplete. allowed-tools limits what the command may use.

The /review command is the most important prompt in the repository, because CI reuses its criteria verbatim.
9dddb4e4d5:
Three design choices answer tasks 4.1 and 4.2 directly.

  • The categories are a closed list with a "report when" condition for each. "Is this a finding?" becomes a check rather than a judgement about general quality.
  • There's an explicit "Do NOT report" section. False positives are what make developers stop reading review bots.
  • The examples sit at the boundary: a parameterised query (no finding), a concatenated ORDER BY (finding), and a double that's display-only (no finding).

Examples of obvious cases teach nothing. The ambiguous ones carry the signal.
d594f944ab:
A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md plus any scripts and templates it needs. The description tells Claude when to use it automatically. Users can also invoke it by name.

The key frontmatter for the exam is context: fork. The skill runs in a separate sub-agent context, and only its final output returns to the main conversation.
9140039b42:
An audit reads dozens of files. Without the fork, every file it opened would sit in the main conversation for the rest of the session. That pushes out the context the developer actually needs. With the fork, the main conversation gets a 30-row table.

It's the same reason you run a batch report in a separate worker instead of inside the request thread.
d3e92da0ff:
Subagents are the tool for independence. security-reviewer has read-only tools and a prompt that says "you did not write this code".

It starts with its own context. So it doesn't carry the reasoning the main session used to generate the code, which is exactly the bias that makes self-review weak.
7e9e5c10b8:
Task 3.4 is plan mode versus direct execution. Plan mode lets Claude explore and propose without editing.

Use it when the change crosses several layers or has more than one reasonable design. "Add order cancellation with a reason code across API, service, migration and UI" touches four areas, plus a migration that can't be undone casually.

Use direct execution for a well-specified local change: "rename placedAt to createdAt in OrderTable.tsx and its test".

The exam distractors sit at the two extremes. Planning everything is slow and pointless for a one-line fix. Planning nothing gives you an unreviewed multi-file migration.
fcf971cc02:
Iterative refinement is a loop. Give Claude a target it can check, let it run, and correct it with concrete evidence. The most reliable target is a failing test.

The repository is set up for that loop. The allow list lets Claude run ./gradlew test and npm test without prompts. The test-writer agent writes tests first. And each React component has a colocated test that doubles as its specification.
8a92417b35:
When the result is wrong, give a concrete example, not an adjective. "The badge colours are off" leads to guessing. "For CANCELLED the badge must have role status and the text 'Cancelled'; the second test fails with: expected 'CANCELLED'" leads to one targeted edit.

The same goes for review criteria. Adding the boundary example for display-only double did more than any amount of "be careful about false positives".
4a811c6787:
In CI there's no human at the terminal.

  • claude -p "prompt" runs one non-interactive session and exits.
  • --output-format json wraps the result in an envelope with fields such as is_error, result, session_id and num_turns.
  • --json-schema asks Claude Code to return output that matches a JSON Schema, placed in structured_output.

Together they turn a review into data that a script can validate, filter and post. (Flag names and envelope fields are as of the time of writing. Check claude --help for your version.)
f74ad8672e: The schema encodes the review criteria. rule_id is an enum of exactly the categories in /review. So a "STYLE-9: consider renaming" finding fails validation instead of reaching the PR. additionalProperties: false keeps the output shape stable. line is an integer of at least 1, so the comment can anchor to a real line.
92cf719253:
Why one call per file? Task 4.6 describes the symptom precisely. One large review of many files is detailed on some, superficial on others, and sometimes contradicts itself. Attention is spread across everything in the context.

A larger context window doesn't fix that. Giving each file its own session does, because each review now has one job.

The cost is that per-file sessions can't see cross-file problems, such as a field renamed in the DTO but not in web/src/types.ts. So a second, integration pass receives the per-file findings and looks only for those. It has its own rule id, XF-1.
1fd6889232:
Why fresh sessions? Every call is a new claude -p with no --resume or --continue.

Suppose Claude generated the code in a developer's session. Reviewing it inside that same session means reviewing with the generator's assumptions already loaded. An independent instance reads the code as a stranger would. The workflow runs the review as its own job for the same reason.
5801f396ed:
Deduplication answers the most common CI complaint: the bot posts the same five comments on every push.

Line numbers are useless for identity. They shift with every commit, and the model rephrases slightly between runs. So the fingerprint is file, rule id and a normalised title (lower case, punctuation removed).

The workflow downloads the previous run's findings.json artifact, passes it as --prior, and uploads the union for the next run. A second run on unchanged code posts nothing.
fc35ea2f44:
Note what the workflow doesn't do. It doesn't give the reviewer Edit or Bash. It doesn't use --dangerously-skip-permissions. It doesn't resume a session.

It does gate the review on the tooling tests. A broken hook or a schema typo stops the pipeline before any tokens are spent. And --fail-on high makes high-severity findings fail the check, which turns review output into something branch protection can act on.
e88f6b254e: If you prefer to see the whole flow on one screen, scripts/multipass_review.sh does the same with bash and jq, minus dedupe and posting:
a207e77d94:
A CI script that calls an LLM is still a program, and most of its bugs are ordinary: wrong flags, missing validation, broken dedupe, posting on error.

You can test all of that without the model. Put a fake claude executable first on PATH. The stub logs its argv, picks a canned payload based on the prompt, and wraps it in the same envelope shape the real CLI returns. Environment variables switch it into failure modes.
85beaf185c: Two traps are planted in the fixtures. The canned integration payload contains a duplicate of a per-file finding, with an exclamation mark added. The prior-findings fixture contains a finding from an earlier run, with a different line number and a trailing full stop. Both must be suppressed.
777316f3d2:
These tests pin down behaviours the exam asks about:

  • the reviewer gets read-only tools;
  • there's no session resumption;
  • there's exactly one session per file, plus one integration session;
  • duplicates are suppressed within and across runs;
  • a CLI error or schema violation raises, instead of posting "no findings".

That last one matters in production. A pipeline that treats a failed review as a clean review is worse than no review. It's the same reason an outage must not become "no orders found" in Capstone A.
3d8f97a325: The repository is a bundle of small decisions about how a team should configure Claude Code and run it in CI. The table states each one, with what it replaced. A team lead defending this setup to a sceptical security reviewer would walk through it row by row.
8373391304:
Hooks receive a JSON description of the pending tool call on standard input. They answer through their exit code and output.

Piping five representative calls through .claude/hooks/guard.py shows all four behaviours the test suite pins, with the real messages the model would see.
cdda8e8f28:
Read the outputs as a design.

  • A destructive shell command is blocked with exit code 2. The stderr message is what the model reads, so it's written as an instruction ("choose a non-destructive alternative").
  • The migration with DROP TABLE is denied with structured JSON. Its reason points at the rule file and the way out (expand and contract), so the model can propose a compliant change instead of retrying.
  • The safe command produces no output and exit 0. That's the silent pass, so the hook adds no noise to normal work.
  • Malformed input exits 1: a non-blocking error.

That last choice is deliberate. If the guard crashes on an input it doesn't understand, you don't want every tool call blocked. The test test_guard_hook.py pins it, so nobody changes it by accident.

The reverse failure is a guard that fails open on a real attack. That's why the declarative deny rules exist as a second layer for the worst cases (rm -rf, .env, curl, force push).
77e79a3925: Hook output formats and exit-code semantics are a documented contract, and they change between Claude Code versions. Check the hooks reference before relying on a field name. The repository pins its assumptions in tests, so a version change shows up as a failing test.
32a354a387:
The suite is small, and it tests tooling, not application code: 33 test functions that expand to 71 cases once parametrised.

The counts: test_guard_hook.py 11 functions, test_findings_schema.py 7, test_review_pipeline.py 9, test_rules_globs.py 6. For each, the interesting question is what silent failure it prevents.
3e0bd0c16b:
scripts/review.py does four things, in order:

  1. It runs one fresh claude -p session per changed file. Each gets read-only tools (Read,Grep,Glob), the review criteria from review.md pasted into the prompt, and the JSON schema supplied with --json-schema.
  2. It runs one integration pass. That pass sees the changed-file list and the per-file findings, and looks only for cross-file problems: a DTO field renamed in one file but not its consumer, a contract change without a test update. It tags them XF-1.
  3. It validates every result against schemas/findings.json.
  4. It removes findings already reported, using a fingerprint of the file, the rule id and the normalised title. Line shifts and punctuation changes don't make an old finding look new.
4beae796ed:
The tests give the numbers.

For two changed files, the pipeline makes three calls: two per-file, one integration. Each has -p, --output-format json, --json-schema and --allowedTools Read,Grep,Glob, and neither --resume nor --continue.

With the canned responses, a run produces 5 raw findings, 4 new, 1 suppressed. (The integration pass repeats a SEC-2 finding already reported by the per-file pass.) Run again with the prior-findings artifact and 2 are suppressed, including one about a missing unit test. So the developer doesn't see the same comments after pushing a fix to something else.

The main entry point returns exit code 1 if any new finding is high severity (--fail-on high is the default). That's what makes the job a gate. With --post, it comments on the pull request through gh.
7b7ff7a854:
Be honest about the limits. The exam and a security reviewer will both ask.

  • The per-file loop in review() runs sequentially, so wall-clock time grows with the number of files. Running the passes concurrently, with a bound, is an easy extension and a good exercise.
  • The integration pass sees findings and the diff, not a full re-read of each file. A defect that only shows when two files are read together, and that no per-file reviewer flagged, can be missed.
  • The dedupe key doesn't understand semantic equivalence. If the model rewords a finding on the second run, it's reported again.
  • The review is only as good as review.md. The explicit report and do-not-report tables are what keep false positives low (task 4.1). Changing them is a code change that deserves review.
d5c9ad3acd:
The Java side is intentionally ordinary: a records-based Spring Boot 3 order service, a @WebMvcTest slice per endpoint, constructor injection, an ApiExceptionHandler.

What's unusual is that the conventions making it ordinary are written down where the tool can read them. The rules say what a senior reviewer says in code review ("no field @Autowired", "return 201 with a Location header"). The review criteria say what to flag and what to leave to the formatter.

For a team with many Spring services, the practical benefit is that the checklist stops living in people's heads. The practical risk is that a rule file is now production configuration. Review it as you'd review a build script, and test it.
3e6139b910: Parallelise the per-file pass with a bounded thread pool (for example, four workers). Measure the wall-clock difference on a 20-file change. What happens to the order of findings, and to the integration prompt?
52004465ec: Add a --max-files guard. When a PR touches more than 25 files, it falls back to reviewing only files in changed packages and posts a note saying so. Where should that note be recorded, so a reader doesn't assume full coverage?
255cc5ca42: Add a second reviewer pass with a different model, and merge the findings. How do you attribute a finding to its source? How do you deduplicate across the two?
dbc4a738fc: Automated tests prove the deterministic parts. The guided exercises (in the repository README) prove the model-facing parts, in a real Claude Code session. Together, they're the definition of done.
6f76ac96ab:
Situation. A platform team adopted Claude Code three months ago. The lead reports four things:

  • (1) Two new hires say Claude writes React tests with getByTestId everywhere, while senior developers' Claude uses role queries.
  • (2) The CI review bot posts between 8 and 12 comments per push, many repeated, and developers have muted it.
  • (3) On a 14-file PR, the bot gave detailed comments on the first three files and nothing on the rest.
  • (4) Last week, Claude in a developer's session ran git push --force after a rebase.

Which changes, in what order?
9a656fe4fa: Invariant first. Add Bash(git push --force:*) to permissions.deny in the committed .claude/settings.json. Add a PreToolUse hook that catches the other spellings (-f, --force-with-lease, +refspec). Reject "add a line to CLAUDE.md": the senior developers probably had one already.
ab2387e5c5: Find where the test conventions live. The senior developers' behaviour suggests the conventions sit in their user-scope ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Move them into .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]. Now they load for everyone, and only when tests are edited. Confirm with /memory on a new hire's machine.
1a6e873e57: Fix review noise. Replace the open-ended review prompt with explicit categories, a do-not-report list and boundary examples (4.1, 4.2). Constrain the output with --json-schema, whose rule_id enum matches the categories. Persist findings as an artifact and dedupe by fingerprint (3.6).
3544fda8ed: Fix uneven depth. Split the single review call into one fresh session per file, plus one integration pass (4.6). Reject "use a bigger model" and "raise max tokens". The cause is attention dilution, not capacity.
2ee87f937f: Prove it. Add the offline tests from this chapter, so future edits to hooks, rules or the schema can't regress silently. Then run the review twice on the same PR and confirm the second run posts nothing new.
2af0854ba6:
The exam versions of this story ask about one item at a time. The pattern to spot is that each symptom names its layer:

  • "only some developers" points at scope;
  • "every push" points at state outside the model;
  • "some files" points at attention;
  • "must never" points at enforcement.
8d5cfd0a92: Copy the repository, create a venv, run pip install -r requirements-dev.txt, then run pytest -q. Done when all 71 tests pass with no network and no API key.
e33da14eff: Break a glob: change testing.md to paths: ["*.test.tsx"]. Done when test_testing_rule_covers_every_colocated_test_in_repo fails and you can explain why. Then restore it.
567ebc6f16: With a real API key, run scripts/multipass_review.sh origin/main on a branch that adds double total to Order and a catch (Exception e) {}. Done when you get COR-1 and COR-3, and no style findings.
